added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: some CTAs will take basically binary positions, so they'll you know, they'll they'll kind of go from fully short to fully long
added_claims.claim: CTAs differ in how position size follows the trend signal: some take binary full-long or full-short positions, while others scale continuously with forecast strength; binary systems get much less benefit from forecast scaling when a trend ends abruptly.
added_claims.conditions: Design choice that decides exposure in a parabolic move.
added_claims.testable: yes - binary versus continuous forecast scaling can be backtested

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: I have a daily rebalance, so I didn't do any trading in silver during Friday itself cuz my position was based on Thursday's close
added_claims.claim: A daily-rebalanced system sizes positions from the prior close, so on a gap day such as 30 Jan 2026 it cannot reduce exposure intraday; the loss is limited only because volatility-scaling had already cut the position in the days before.
added_claims.indicator: daily rebalance using previous close, silver
added_claims.direction: position cut ahead of the crash by earlier volatility rises
added_claims.conditions: Gap risk remains for any end-of-day system; only earlier vol-scaling protects it.
added_claims.testable: yes - execution lag and gap losses are measurable

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: I guess you could have also been stopped out on freaky Friday because the move was so big
added_claims.claim: A trader using a hard stop based on the recent high (possibly vol-linked) could have been stopped out on the crash day itself, so whether a stop-loss rule helps in a parabolic reversal depends on its exact definition.
added_claims.indicator: stop-loss defined from the recent high
added_claims.direction: stop triggers on a large one-day fall
added_claims.conditions: Depends on the stop rule and its volatility multiple.
added_claims.testable: partly - stop rules can be backtested for gap days

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: a 25% fall probably still would have breached any reasonable stop
added_claims.claim: Even a volatility-widened stop would probably have been breached by a 25% one-day fall, so stops do not remove gap risk; the size of the position, not the stop, determines the loss.
added_claims.conditions: Gap moves bypass stops, so sizing is the main protection.
added_claims.testable: yes - gap size versus stop distance is measurable

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: maybe become a little bit complacent thinking that these are all the same to trade
added_claims.claim: After a long rally in precious metals, traders can become complacent and assume silver and platinum are as liquid as gold, but they are different markets with different liquidity and crash risk.
added_claims.indicator: silver and platinum versus gold liquidity
added_claims.direction: liquidity risk underestimated in the less liquid metals
added_claims.testable: partly - liquidity differences across metals can be measured

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: I might kind of have a fairly broad liquidity filter
added_claims.claim: A small account can use a broader liquidity filter than large CTAs and so holds instruments that big CTAs avoid or hold small, which gives it extra markets but also more exposure to thin-market liquidity gaps.
added_claims.indicator: liquidity filter relative to account size
added_claims.conditions: Small accounts only; capacity limits large CTAs.
added_claims.testable: yes - liquidity filter thresholds can be set from volume and open interest

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: if confirmed, we will have a new Fed chair with the name of Kevin Walsh
added_claims.claim: Kevin Warsh was named as the nominee for Fed chair around the time of the 30 January 2026 silver crash, a surprise relative to expectations, and was taken by many as the proximate cause of the precious-metals sell-off.
added_claims.direction: tighter policy narrative for precious metals
added_claims.conditions: Time-bound event; the speakers doubt it was the real cause.

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: he does he does have some opinions that are less mainstream around things like QE and the Fed balance sheet
added_claims.claim: The Fed chair nominee holds less mainstream views on QE and the Fed balance sheet but is seen as conventional or even hawkish on interest-rate setting, so the policy mix could differ from what the president wants.
added_claims.indicator: Fed balance sheet and QE policy
added_claims.direction: policy uncertainty rather than clear direction
added_claims.conditions: Depends on confirmation and how the board votes.

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: Trump always chickens out of the taco trade
added_claims.claim: Markets have largely shrugged off the president's policy shocks since early 2025, partly because of a 'TACO' pattern (he backs down) and because many do not take threats seriously, so Rob's initial expectation of a bad market was wrong.
added_claims.indicator: equity reaction to tariff and policy announcements
added_claims.conditions: Observed over the first year; may not hold if a shock is not reversed.
added_claims.testable: partly - post-announcement returns can be studied

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: let's not forget it was Trump who appointed Powell
added_claims.claim: A president's appointment says little about a Fed chair's later independence: Powell was appointed by Trump and then resisted pressure, and once in office chairs cannot be removed and care about their legacy.
added_claims.direction: appointee may act against the appointer's wishes
added_claims.conditions: Depends on legal protection of the Fed from removal.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: it's not like he can decide what interest rates are going to do
added_claims.claim: The Fed chair is one of 12 FOMC votes and cannot set rates alone; the real independence risk is a pending Supreme Court ruling that may let the president remove governors and pack the board.
added_claims.indicator: FOMC voting structure, Supreme Court ruling on Fed removal
added_claims.direction: independence risk if the ruling favours the president
added_claims.testable: no - depends on a court ruling

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: my risk is a little bit higher than it has been for a while, so that kind of matches up with your trend barometer
added_claims.claim: A system that scales positions with forecast strength runs higher realised risk when many markets trend strongly, so portfolio risk rises with trend breadth (the barometer).
added_claims.direction: risk rises when breadth of trends is high
added_claims.testable: yes - realised vol versus trend breadth can be tested

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: as long as your correlation estimate's quite slow, like 6 months is pretty good, then that's going to be al- effectively irrelevant
added_claims.claim: Extra trading caused by updating a slow (six-month) correlation estimate is negligible compared with the trading caused by signals, so a time-varying estimate has little cost compared with a fixed assumption.
added_claims.conditions: Slow estimation window of about six months.
added_claims.testable: yes - turnover from estimate changes can be measured

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: this is a paper about not really about better models or faster signals
added_claims.claim: The Man AHL paper argues that differences between trend managers come mainly from which markets they trade (the market universe), not from better models or faster signals.
added_claims.conditions: Paper's central thesis; evidence in factor and idiosyncratic decomposition.
added_claims.testable: yes - testable by comparing universe versus speed contributions

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: that kind of first principal component didn't contribute much
added_claims.claim: January 2026 trend profits did not come from the risk-on/risk-off factor (bonds flat, equities slightly up) but from idiosyncratic sources such as gold, silver and natural gas, an example of returns from alternative-style markets.
added_claims.indicator: first principal component of trend returns, January 2026
added_claims.direction: idiosyncratic metals and gas drove returns
added_claims.testable: yes - PCA decomposition can be repeated on the index

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker. The comment that a 3% one-day loss was in line with other CTAs at similar annual volatility is Niels's, based on what he saw from managers he follows; Rob only reported his own 3% loss.
corrections.fix: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen: a 3% loss on the crash day was very decent for a trend manager at that annual volatility, matching what he saw from the managers he can follow.

completeness_estimate: 0.84 - first reader captured the silver crash mechanics, sizing and paper findings well; missed side mechanisms (binary versus continuous sizing, daily-rebalance gap, stop-loss gap risk, liquidity filter, Fed chair institutional points, TACO behaviour, correlation-turnover point)
